question: Can a finite-width, one-layer linear state-space language model reproduce the next-token distribution of any finite n-gram language model, and can that construction explain what gradient-trained SSMs remember on a small synthetic language?

key_findings.claim: For a fixed finite language and n-gram rule set P, the paper constructs a one-hidden-layer SSM language model with |P| hidden units whose softmax output is arbitrarily close in L1 distance to the n-gram model on valid prefixes.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.1 states epsilon-equivalence for any positive epsilon, any embedding dimension at least one, and a hidden layer containing one unit per valid (n-1)-word context. The use of epsilon, rather than exact equivalence, accounts for softmax assigning positive probability to every vocabulary item.

anchors.section: Appendix A.3, proofs of Proposition 4.4 and Theorem 4.3

key_findings.claim: The core representation argument reduces next-token prediction to finite sequence memorization and gives a constructive K-hidden-unit SSM interpolant for K distinct sequence-to-vector pairs.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4.5 chooses the recurrence and input matrices so the ReLU-transformed final hidden states are linearly independent, then chooses the output matrix to map those states to arbitrary targets. The appendix obtains independence by making every coordinate pairwise distinct and selecting output biases that yield a nonsingular ReLU feature matrix.

anchors.section: Appendix A.1, Lemma A.4 and proof of Proposition 4.5

key_findings.claim: An exactly nilpotent state-transition matrix provides an exact finite context window: if A to the nth power is zero, inputs older than n steps cannot affect the final state.
key_findings.evidence: Unrolling the linear recurrence expresses the last hidden state as a sum of powers of A applied to prior inputs. All terms at lag n or greater vanish when A^n=0. The n-gram construction applies this with order n-1 so only the required (n-1)-token context remains.

key_findings.claim: The empirical study is a small consistency demonstration, not a test of the general theorem at realistic language-model scale.
key_findings.evidence: The only reported task uses a hand-built 4-gram language with 145 valid trigram contexts and hundreds of templated sentences. A 10-dimensional embedding and 145-unit SSM are trained for 25 epochs at learning rate 0.001; over five random seeds, 40 training sentences are said to produce near-perfect accuracy on six-token prefixes, but the paper prints no exact accuracy, variance, split size, or baseline result.

key_findings.claim: The learned-spectrum evidence does not establish the paper's exact finite-memory mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: The trained SSM has all but one reported eigenvalue inside the unit disk, whereas the theorem requires exact nilpotency and hence all eigenvalues exactly zero. A single eigenvalue outside the unit disk also prevents powers of A from converging to zero in general, so the plot is at most suggestive of mostly decaying modes, not confirmation of the construction.

anchors.section: 5.2 Spectral decomposition of hidden weight matrices

key_findings.claim: The representation visualization is qualitatively compatible with n-gram clustering but is internally under-specified.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 projects hidden states with PCA and visually groups prefixes sharing their final trigram. However, Section 5.1 specifies a 145-unit hidden layer while Section 5.3 calls the plotted embeddings 64-dimensional, and it reports no cluster metric, comparison to random features, or relationship between cluster tightness and held-out next-token error.

anchors.section: Figure 4 and 5.3 Hidden embeddings for n-grams

key_findings.claim: The paper proves containment of finite n-gram language models, not strict superiority over them or learnability by gradient descent.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.1 is an existence result showing that an SSM can approximate each fixed n-gram model. It does not exhibit an SSM distribution outside the n-gram class under the same resource constraints, prove that optimization finds the constructed weights, or bound sample complexity. The discussion explicitly leaves SGD convergence and generalization as future work.

key_findings.claim: The RNN extension is a proposed transfer of proof ingredients rather than a theorem matching the SSM result.
key_findings.evidence: The main text says it expects the memorization proposition to extend to RNNs. Appendix A.4 proves only the finite-window lemma under a specially defined block-nilpotent recurrent matrix and sketches how sufficiently large biases could make the nonlinear update locally linear for a memorization argument.

method.core_idea: Encode every valid n-gram context as one member of a finite sequence-to-output interpolation problem, use a nilpotent linear recurrence to erase older inputs, and choose a ReLU readout that maps the remaining context state to the desired next-token logits.
method.mechanism: Words are mapped through any injective embedding. A linear recurrence accumulates the embedded sequence. Generic recurrence and input matrices, constrained so a fixed power of the recurrence is zero, make the final states of the finite context set coordinate-wise distinct. Carefully chosen ReLU biases turn those states into a linearly independent feature matrix; a linear output layer then interpolates smoothed n-gram log-probabilities. Softmax converts the logits to an epsilon-close distribution. The empirical section trains an architecture with the theorem's one-unit-per-context width and inspects its eigenvalues and PCA-projected hidden states.
assumptions: The vocabulary, maximum sentence length, language, and set of valid n-gram contexts are finite and fixed before constructing the model.
All embedded context sequences are distinct, which follows only if the learned or chosen embedding retains word identity.
Arbitrary real-valued parameters and sufficiently precise arithmetic are available for the generic-position and interpolation construction.
A bias is permitted before the ReLU output feature map, although many practical SSM parameterizations omit this term.
Approximation on valid prefixes of the chosen language is the target; behavior on invalid or out-of-language prefixes is not constrained by epsilon-equivalence.
An existence construction with K hidden units and O(K^2) parameters is an informative model of what gradient descent learns.
Eigenvalues mostly inside the unit disk and visible PCA clusters are useful qualitative proxies for exact nilpotency and rule encoding.

techniques.role: Recasts n-gram next-token prediction as interpolation over the finite set of valid (n-1)-token contexts.
Forces exact forgetting beyond a chosen lag by constraining a power of the state-transition matrix to zero.
Selects biases that make ReLU-transformed hidden states linearly independent, allowing a linear readout to memorize arbitrary target logits.
Replaces zero n-gram probabilities with small positive values so finite logits can approximate the target distribution.
Inspects learned recurrence eigenvalues as a qualitative probe of how quickly old input directions decay.
Uses PCA to ask whether prefixes with the same final trigram occupy nearby hidden representations.

evaluations.setting: A synthetic two-template English-like 4-gram language with 145 valid trigram contexts and hundreds of possible sentences
evaluations.metric: Whether completion of each held-out six-token prefix produces a sentence belonging to the generated language
evaluations.result: The authors report consistently near-perfect accuracy from five random seeds when trained on 40 sentences, without printing exact values or dispersion
evaluations.baseline: No n-gram, RNN, transformer, width, or unconstrained-SSM baseline is numerically reported

evaluations.setting: The learned state-transition matrix of the toy SSM
evaluations.metric: Eigenvalue locations relative to the unit disk
evaluations.result: All plotted eigenvalues except one are reported inside the unit circle
evaluations.baseline: The theorem's exact construction requires a nilpotent matrix whose eigenvalues are all zero; no nilpotency-regularized or random-matrix control is shown

evaluations.metric: Qualitative separation in a two-dimensional PCA projection by final trigram
evaluations.result: Same-trigram states appear in visual clusters in Figure 4
evaluations.baseline: No quantitative clustering score, random-feature control, alternative projection, or error-conditioned comparison is reported

limitations: Author-stated: the K-unit, O(K^2)-parameter memorization construction is not parameter-optimal; extending tight O(K)-parameter feed-forward results to recurrent state-space models remains open.
Author-stated: fixed-order n-grams cannot model full English without a prohibitive number of rules, so more expressive formal grammars are needed for realistic language structure.
Author-stated: the theory does not establish that stochastic gradient descent discovers the construction or generalizes from n-gram samples without overparameterization.
Author-stated: practical long-memory SSMs such as S4 and Mamba use structures outside the simple one-layer, time-invariant model analyzed here.
Reviewer-identified: the theorem is a representational existence result on valid prefixes, not a strict separation showing SSMs are more expressive than n-gram models.
Reviewer-identified: the empirical dataset is tiny and templated, exact scores and split sizes are omitted, and there are no numerical baselines or uncertainty estimates.

Reviewer-identified: the learned matrix is not shown to be nilpotent; an eigenvalue outside the unit disk conflicts with the claimed approximate-decay interpretation unless its mode is inaccessible or cancelled, which is not tested.
Reviewer-identified: the hidden width is reported as both 145 and 64 in the experimental description, leaving the PCA analysis's source representation ambiguous.
Reviewer-identified: the construction relies on generic real-valued weights and exact linear independence without a robustness margin, finite-precision bound, or perturbation analysis.
Reviewer-identified: the RNN memorization extension is sketched but not stated and proved at the same level as the SSM theorem.
failure_modes: A nearly nilpotent learned recurrence can retain a weak unstable mode indefinitely, so eigenvalues that look mostly contractive need not implement a clean finite context window.
Finite-precision rounding can destroy the narrow separation between generic hidden coordinates or make the ReLU feature matrix ill-conditioned, requiring impractically large output weights.
When the number of observed n-gram contexts grows with vocabulary and order, the one-unit-per-rule construction and quadratic parameter count become infeasible.
A model can memorize all contexts represented in a templated train split while failing on unseen lexical combinations, invalid contexts, longer prefixes, or a shifted n-gram distribution.
PCA can visually merge or separate clusters because of projection choice even when the full hidden geometry does not support a stable context decoder.
Softmax approximation can assign nonzero mass to forbidden tokens; reducing epsilon may require increasingly extreme logits and worsen numerical conditioning.
Modern selective or input-dependent SSM layers need not obey the fixed linear recurrence assumptions, so conclusions about their mechanisms may not transfer.
reusable_insights: Turn a finite-rule sequence task into a representation-plus-interpolation problem: first prove that each relevant context gets a distinct stable state, then solve the output map separately.
Use algebraic structure in the recurrence to encode a memory policy; nilpotency is an exact finite-window design, while spectral radius controls only asymptotic decay.
Separate representability, optimization, and generalization claims. An explicit weight construction answers the first but gives no guarantee for the latter two.
Audit learned-mechanism claims by comparing the trained object to every necessary condition of the constructive proof, not only a visually similar spectrum or embedding plot.
When softmax prevents exact zeros, state the approximation metric and analyze how the required logit scale changes with target error.
For synthetic formal-language experiments, publish full generators, exact split cardinalities, length extrapolation tests, numerical baselines, and seed-level results.
open_questions: Can a robust version of the memorization theorem bound the minimum singular value of the ReLU feature matrix under finite precision and bounded parameter norms?
What regularizer or parameterization makes gradient descent learn an approximately finite-window recurrence without leaving unstable eigenmodes?
Can the construction be reduced from O(K^2) to O(K) parameters for SSMs while preserving an explicit context-window constraint?
Does the claimed rule representation survive length extrapolation, larger vocabularies, stochastic n-gram distributions, and held-out context combinations?
How does the result change for diagonal, complex, selective, gated, or input-dependent state-space layers used in Mamba-like models?
Can strict expressivity beyond every fixed-order n-gram family be shown under bounded width, bounded precision, and a resource-matched comparison?
Which full-space probe can establish that learned hidden states encode the last n-1 tokens causally rather than merely correlate with them in a PCA view?
Can a formally verified block-nilpotent RNN extension be proved without making the nonlinear recurrence effectively linear through large biases?

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Can Represent n-gram Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Svete and Cotterell construct transformer language models that exactly represent any n-gram model using hard or sparse attention. The present paper instead constructs a one-layer recurrent SSM with softmax epsilon-approximation and an explicit nilpotent finite-memory mechanism; it does not compare resource requirements or optimization between the two constructions.

competitive_landscape.title: The Expressive Capacity of State Space Models: A Formal Language Perspective
competitive_landscape.difference: Sarrof, Veitsman, and Hahn characterize positive and negative capabilities of practical SSM families over star-free regular languages, counters, and bounded hierarchy, with Mamba experiments and finite-precision considerations. The present paper gives a narrower finite n-gram distribution construction with an explicit |P|-unit bound but does not characterize the wider language class or modern gate constraints.

competitive_landscape.title: The Illusion of State in State-Space Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Merrill, Petty, and Sabharwal prove circuit-complexity limits for bounded-depth SSMs and show Mamba-style models struggle with state tracking such as permutation composition. Those limits concern length-growing sequential computation; they do not contradict memorizing a fixed finite n-gram context set, but they sharply limit extrapolating the present construction to general state tracking.

competitive_landscape.title: Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying
competitive_landscape.difference: Jelassi and colleagues prove and measure a transformer advantage over fixed-state generalized SSMs on copying and retrieval as sequence length grows. The present paper studies local finite-context rules, where deliberate forgetting is sufficient; it therefore cannot support a broad claim that SSMs dominate attention on sequence expressivity.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Expressivity of Selective State-Space Layers: A Multivariate Polynomial Approach
competitive_landscape.difference: Cohen-Karlik and colleagues analyze the input-selective S6 layer through multivariate polynomial degree and compare it with linear attention, including empirical checks on simplified Mamba variants. The present paper analyzes a fixed linear recurrence plus ReLU readout and n-gram interpolation, so its proof does not cover the selectivity mechanism responsible for modern Mamba expressivity.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents the first explicit finite-width construction showing that a one-layer state-space language model can encode any fixed n-gram rule system, together with a new SSM memorization-capacity result and a nilpotent-spectrum account of finite context.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Theorem 4.1 gives an |P|-hidden-unit epsilon-representation for a finite n-gram model; Proposition 4.5 constructs arbitrary finite sequence interpolation with K hidden units; Proposition 4.6 ties exact forgetting to A^n=0. A small synthetic experiment reports near-perfect completion and qualitative spectrum and clustering plots.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the combination of an explicit size bound, a sequence-memorization lemma for this simple SSM, and a nilpotent finite-window construction for probabilistic n-gram prediction. It is not a strict proof that SSMs are more expressive than n-gram models, a theory of how SGD learns the construction, or a characterization of Mamba. Transformer n-gram representation, broader formal-language SSM results, circuit-complexity limits, copying separations, and selective-SSM polynomial analyses now surround and narrow the claim. The paper remains useful as a clean constructive lower bound, but its empirical mechanism evidence is qualitative and contains width and spectral ambiguities.

reviewer_notes: Primary full-text pass read all 23 pages of the pinned TMLR February 2025 extraction on 2026-08-23, including the complete proofs in Appendix A and all 145 listed trigram contexts in Appendix B. Author claims and reviewer inferences are labeled per finding. Quantitative descriptions preserve the paper's own under-specification: 'near-perfect' has no printed score or variance. Current primary records were checked across three query families: n-gram representation, formal-language/state-tracking limits, and selective-SSM expressivity. The learned-spectrum claim was narrowed because one eigenvalue outside the unit disk cannot generally support powers of A approaching zero, and the PCA discussion was flagged because the experimental hidden width is described as both 145 and 64.
